articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
articles.content:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.

The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.

The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.

Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.

Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.

Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.

The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.

"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.

"You just have to prepare it in the right way.

"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.

"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.

"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."

Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin

Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.

Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.

The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.

Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.

"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."

Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.

The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light

To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.

Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.

"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."

The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.

This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.

As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.

The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.

"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.

Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications

The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.

One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.

The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.

Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.

Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.

"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.

"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.

"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.

"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.

These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.

A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed

For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.

By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.

The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.

"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.

"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."

The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about light's intrinsic geometric properties that enables new ways to manipulate light without external materials. This breakthrough has broad potential applications in medical diagnostics, secure communications, and quantum technologies, representing a meaningful advance with wide societal impact. The article provides detailed context and explains the discovery's implications clearly.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.summary: Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
articles.content:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.

The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.

The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.

A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959

In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.

In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.

Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.

The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.

Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.

These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.

The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.

Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.

How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment

The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.

Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.

The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.

The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.

By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.

Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.

Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution

The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.

Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.

Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.

Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.

"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."

What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.

A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion

With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.

Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.

When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.

Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.

The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.

This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.

The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.

A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics

The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.

The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.

Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.

Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.

By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.

The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough where Oxford physicists successfully recreated the Aharonov-Bohm quantum effect using a hybrid quantum computer. This achievement advances quantum simulation technology, enabling deeper exploration of fundamental physics phenomena that are difficult to study with classical computers. The impact is broad for science and technology, with potential long-term benefits for quantum computing and understanding of quantum mechanics.

articles.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
articles.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.
articles.content:
Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish possess some of the most sophisticated nervous systems in the animal kingdom, giving them remarkable abilities such as solving problems and rapidly changing their appearance to blend into their surroundings. But how did these extraordinary capabilities evolve? Scientists have uncovered a surprising clue that may lie not in the genes themselves, but in the way DNA is folded and arranged inside cells.

Researchers at the University of Vienna discovered that a massive reorganization of DNA hundreds of millions of years ago brought previously separated genetic regions into contact. These newly formed connections changed how genes could interact and be controlled, potentially helping drive the evolution of the unusually complex nervous systems found in these animals, which are collectively known as coleoid cephalopods.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest that the physical structure of DNA may play a much more active role in evolution than scientists once thought.

How the 3D Structure of DNA Influences Evolution

To investigate this possibility, the research team reconstructed the three-dimensional organization of the genome in octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish. They then compared the arrangement of DNA with patterns of gene activity to understand how changes in genome structure might influence biological complexity.

"The genome isn't just a sequence of genes. It's folded into a complex three-dimensional structure," said lead author Dr. Thea Rogers. "Understanding how that structure evolves is becoming increasingly important for understanding how new forms of biological complexity arise."

Although DNA is often pictured as a long, twisted ladder, it does not simply stretch out inside a cell. Instead, it folds into an intricate three-dimensional arrangement, allowing sections that are far apart along the DNA sequence to come into close physical contact.

These connections matter because they can influence which genes are activated, when they are used, and how strongly they function. Changes in the way DNA folds can therefore alter gene activity without necessarily changing the underlying genetic instructions.

An Ancient DNA Reshuffling Created New Genetic Connections

The researchers found evidence that cephalopod genomes underwent an extensive period of reorganization hundreds of millions of years ago. During this evolutionary upheaval, large sections of genetic material were rearranged, bringing regions of chromosomes that had previously been separated into close proximity.

This reshuffling created opportunities for DNA regions to interact in ways that had not previously been possible. Once these connections formed, they could influence each other's activity, gradually establishing more elaborate networks of genetic regulation.

Over evolutionary time, the interactions could become increasingly interconnected and difficult to separate, creating a process the scientists describe as "regulatory entanglement."

This mechanism offers a possible explanation for how evolution can produce new biological features without disrupting the essential functions organisms need to survive. By establishing new connections among existing genetic elements, the genome may develop different patterns of gene activity while keeping crucial biological systems intact.

Stable DNA Structures and Flexible Genetic Loops

One of the study's most revealing findings was that different parts of the genome responded very differently to evolutionary reorganization.

The researchers discovered that large structural regions called chromatin domains remained remarkably stable over long periods of evolutionary history. These domains help organize DNA into broad sections within the cell, and their persistence suggests that some features of genome architecture are strongly conserved.

Smaller structures known as chromatin loops, however, told a different story.

These loops form when distant sections of DNA are brought together in three-dimensional space. Unlike the relatively stable chromatin domains, the loops showed substantial differences between cephalopod species, between tissues, and across stages of development.

Particularly intriguing was their location. Many of these flexible DNA connections appeared near genes associated with important cephalopod characteristics, including the development and function of the nervous system.

This pattern suggests that smaller, more adaptable structures within the genome may be especially responsive to major genetic rearrangements. By changing which regions of DNA can communicate, these flexible connections could help generate new patterns of gene activity and contribute to the evolution of complex traits.

A New Clue to the Evolution of Octopus Intelligence

The discovery challenges a traditional view of genome architecture as something that primarily changes in response to evolution. Instead, the findings suggest that the physical organization of DNA can itself influence how evolutionary changes unfold.

In octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish, ancient rearrangements of the genome may have helped establish new regulatory networks that contributed to the development of their exceptionally sophisticated nervous systems.

The results do not establish that these DNA changes directly caused the evolution of cephalopod intelligence. However, they reveal a potential mechanism through which large genetic rearrangements could create new biological possibilities while preserving essential functions.

More broadly, the research points to an often overlooked dimension of evolution. The emergence of extraordinary traits may depend not only on which genes an organism inherits, but also on how those genes are physically arranged and connected within the cell.

articles.personality_title: Ancient DNA reshuffling may explain octopus intelligence
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish are known for their smart behavior and complex nervous systems. Scientists have long wondered how these animals developed such advanced abilities.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of Vienna studied the 3D structure of DNA in these animals. They found that hundreds of millions of years ago, their DNA was rearranged in a way that brought distant parts of the genome closer together. This change may have allowed new interactions between genes, helping to build their complex nervous systems.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that the physical folding of DNA inside cells can affect evolution. Instead of just changes in the genes themselves, how DNA is organized can create new ways for genes to work together. This could explain how cephalopods evolved their intelligence without losing important functions.

**What's next step** – Scientists will likely study other animals to see if similar DNA folding effects helped their evolution. Understanding these 3D DNA patterns might also improve our knowledge of genetics and how complex traits develop in different species.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The way DNA folds and connects inside cells may have helped octopuses and their relatives evolve their remarkable intelligence by creating new gene interactions.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un ancien réarrangement de l'ADN pourrait expliquer l'intelligence des pieuvres
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les pieuvres, les calmars et les seiches sont connus pour leur comportement intelligent et leurs systèmes nerveux complexes. Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps comment ces animaux ont développé de telles capacités avancées.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'Université de Vienne ont étudié la structure 3D de l'ADN de ces animaux. Ils ont découvert qu'il y a des centaines de millions d'années, leur ADN a été réorganisé de manière à rapprocher des parties éloignées du génome. Ce changement aurait permis de nouvelles interactions entre les gènes, aidant à construire leurs systèmes nerveux complexes.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que le pliage physique de l'ADN dans les cellules peut influencer l'évolution. Au lieu de simples modifications des gènes eux-mêmes, la manière dont l'ADN est organisé peut créer de nouvelles façons pour les gènes de fonctionner ensemble. Cela pourrait expliquer comment les céphalopodes ont développé leur intelligence sans perdre des fonctions importantes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques étudieront probablement d'autres animaux pour voir si des effets similaires du pliage de l'ADN ont aidé leur évolution. Comprendre ces motifs d'ADN en 3D pourrait aussi améliorer nos connaissances en génétique et sur le développement des traits complexes chez différentes espèces.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La façon dont l'ADN se plie et se connecte dans les cellules pourrait avoir aidé les pieuvres et leurs proches à évoluer leur intelligence remarquable en créant de nouvelles interactions génétiques.
articles.personality_title_es: Un antiguo reordenamiento del ADN podría explicar la inteligencia del pulpo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los pulpos, calamares y sepias son conocidos por su comportamiento inteligente y sistemas nerviosos complejos. Los científicos han querido saber cómo estos animales desarrollaron tales habilidades avanzadas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Viena estudiaron la estructura 3D del ADN en estos animales. Descubrieron que hace cientos de millones de años, su ADN se reorganizó para acercar partes distantes del genoma. Este cambio pudo permitir nuevas interacciones entre genes, ayudando a formar sus sistemas nerviosos complejos.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo muestra que el plegamiento físico del ADN dentro de las células puede afectar la evolución. No solo los cambios en los genes, sino también cómo está organizado el ADN puede crear nuevas formas para que los genes trabajen juntos. Esto podría explicar cómo los cefalópodos desarrollaron su inteligencia sin perder funciones importantes.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos probablemente estudiarán otros animales para ver si efectos similares del plegamiento del ADN ayudaron en su evolución. Entender estos patrones de ADN en 3D podría mejorar nuestro conocimiento sobre genética y cómo se desarrollan rasgos complejos en diferentes especies.

**Resumen en una frase** – La forma en que el ADN se pliega y conecta dentro de las células podría haber ayudado a los pulpos y sus parientes a desarrollar su notable inteligencia creando nuevas interacciones genéticas.

articles.title: Is this idea from AI or humans? A detector claims it can tell
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03247-0A tool called IdeaLens helps to judge whether concepts — rather than just writing — in scientific papers are artificially generated.
articles.content:
Credit: EvgeniyShkolenko/Getty

Researchers have developed a detector that aims to tell the difference between ideas made by humans and those conjured by artificial intelligence.

Used with care, IdeaLens could help to gauge the extent of AI use in submissions to conferences and journals, which have become “overwhelmed” with artificially generated content, says Rishanth Rajendhran, a computer scientist at the University of Maryland in College Park and co-author of the preprint1 describing IdeaLens.

Using AI to write scientific papers is becoming increasingly acceptable, but only “as long as the core idea” is the researcher’s own, he says.

Is it OK for AI to write science papers? Nature survey shows researchers are split

The detector works by analysing the ‘outline’ of a work rather than the text itself. First, it distils a text — for example, a scientific paper — into an outline, stripping it of style. Then it looks for patterns that are characteristic of either AI or human-generated ideas, such as in arguments and flow.

The detector was able to spot AI-derived ideas 91% of the time. It “surprised me that they can detect AI-written arguments” from just the outlines, says Nikhil Garg, a computer scientist at Cornell Tech in New York City, who calls the detector impressive.

Garg cautions that because the tool is fallible, it should not be used to judge the human authenticity of individual cases, and that the detector might become inaccurate when used on types of data that are different from those used in training. “An AI ‘tell’ in one domain may simply be good human writing in another,” he says.

Structural differences

The group’s earlier work found that human-written stories differ structurally from those written by AI and that different chatbots tend to use the same arguments when writing essays. Together this suggested that it might be possible to make a detector for AI ideas, says Rajendhran.

articles.personality_title: New tool can spot AI-generated scientific ideas with high accuracy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to help write research papers. While this is becoming more accepted, many want to make sure that the main ideas in these papers come from humans, not AI.

**What happened** – Researchers created a tool called IdeaLens that can tell if the main ideas in scientific papers were made by humans or AI. Instead of looking at the words, it studies the structure and flow of the ideas. The tool was tested and correctly identified AI-generated ideas 91% of the time.

**Impact** – This tool is important because it helps keep research honest by checking if AI is being used too much to create ideas. It can be used by journals and conferences to understand how much AI is influencing new scientific work. However, experts warn it shouldn’t be used to judge single papers since it might make mistakes.

**What's next step** – The researchers hope IdeaLens will be improved and used more widely to support fair science publishing. They also want to study how well it works with different kinds of research papers and in other fields.

**One-sentence takeaway** – IdeaLens is a new tool that helps tell if scientific ideas come from humans or AI by analyzing their structure, supporting honest research.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouvel outil détecte avec précision les idées scientifiques générées par l'IA
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques utilisent de plus en plus l'intelligence artificielle (IA) pour aider à rédiger des articles de recherche. Bien que cela soit de plus en plus accepté, beaucoup souhaitent s'assurer que les idées principales de ces articles viennent des humains, pas de l'IA.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont créé un outil appelé IdeaLens qui peut déterminer si les idées principales dans les articles scientifiques ont été créées par des humains ou par l'IA. Au lieu d'examiner les mots, il étudie la structure et le déroulement des idées. L'outil a été testé et a identifié correctement les idées générées par l'IA dans 91 % des cas.

**Impact** – Cet outil est important car il aide à maintenir l'honnêteté dans la recherche en vérifiant si l'IA est trop utilisée pour créer des idées. Il peut être utilisé par les revues et les conférences pour comprendre dans quelle mesure l'IA influence les nouveaux travaux scientifiques. Cependant, des experts avertissent qu'il ne faut pas l'utiliser pour juger des articles individuels car il peut faire des erreurs.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs espèrent qu'IdeaLens sera amélioré et utilisé plus largement pour soutenir une publication scientifique équitable. Ils veulent aussi étudier son efficacité avec différents types d'articles de recherche et dans d'autres domaines.

**Résumé en une phrase** – IdeaLens est un nouvel outil qui aide à distinguer si les idées scientifiques viennent des humains ou de l'IA en analysant leur structure, soutenant ainsi une recherche honnête.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva herramienta detecta con alta precisión ideas científicas generadas por IA
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos usan cada vez más la inteligencia artificial (IA) para ayudar a escribir artículos de investigación. Aunque esto es más aceptado, muchos quieren asegurarse de que las ideas principales en estos artículos provengan de humanos, no de la IA.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores crearon una herramienta llamada IdeaLens que puede decir si las ideas principales en los artículos científicos fueron hechas por humanos o IA. En lugar de mirar las palabras, estudia la estructura y el flujo de las ideas. La herramienta fue probada y reconoció correctamente ideas generadas por IA el 91% de las veces.

**Impacto** – Esta herramienta es importante porque ayuda a mantener la honestidad en la investigación al verificar si se usa demasiado la IA para crear ideas. Puede ser usada por revistas y conferencias para entender cuánto influye la IA en nuevos trabajos científicos. Sin embargo, expertos advierten que no debe usarse para juzgar casos individuales porque puede equivocarse.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan que IdeaLens mejore y se use más para apoyar una publicación científica justa. También quieren estudiar qué tan bien funciona con distintos tipos de artículos y en otras áreas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – IdeaLens es una nueva herramienta que ayuda a saber si las ideas científicas vienen de humanos o IA analizando su estructura, apoyando la investigación honesta.
